content: Ichthyosis vulgaris is a dermatological condition characterized by dry, scaly skin. It is the most prevalent form of ichthyosis, affecting approximately 1 in 250 individuals, which is why it is often referred to as common ichthyosis. Due to its appearance, it is also colloquially known as fish skin disease. The condition is predominantly inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, frequently associated with mutations in the filaggrin gene. However, there is a very rare non-inherited variant known as acquired ichthyosis vulgaris. Epidemiologically, ichthyosis vulgaris is the most common type of ichthyosis, with a prevalence of about 1 in 250 people. Environmental factors play a significant role in the severity of the condition. For individuals with severe cases, the climate in which they reside can have a profound impact. Paradoxically, those prone to prickly itch are advised to seek out hot and humid climates rather than avoid them. Living in a tropical climate year-round promotes sweating, which helps clear the scales and mitigates the risk of prickly itch. Conversely, cold and dry climates exacerbate the condition by inhibiting sweating and contributing to the accumulation of scales. Harsh winters, excessive exposure to strong air-conditioning, and overconsumption of alcohol can further aggravate the buildup of scales and increase the likelihood of prickly itch. The symptoms of inherited ichthyosis vulgaris typically become apparent around the age of four. These symptoms often improve with age but may worsen again in older adulthood. In contrast, the acquired variant usually manifests during adulthood. While the condition is not life-threatening, individuals with mild cases may experience mild itching and social discomfort due to the unusual appearance of their skin. Symptoms in mild cases include mosaic lines or scaly patches on the shins, fine white scales on the forearms, and rough palms. Severe cases, though rare, involve widespread scaling, with areas rich in sweat glands being the least affected. Regions where the skin folds or rubs against itself, such as the armpits, groin, and flexural areas of the elbows and knees, are also less affected. In severe cases, the accumulation of scales can lead to prickly itch, particularly when the individual needs to sweat but is unable to do so due to the scales. Treatment options primarily involve topical therapies designed to exfoliate the scales. These include lotions containing alpha-hydroxy acids, which help to remove the accumulated scales and improve the skin's appearance and texture.
